learn: Fluent readers read accurately, at a good pace and with expression, so their reading sounds like talking.
Fluency matters because when you don't have to work hard on every word, your brain can focus on meaning.
Rereading a passage several times, and reading aloud with a partner, are proven ways to build fluency.
check: What are the three parts of fluency?
Your brain can focus on meaning
lessons.try: Read the same paragraph aloud three times. Notice how it gets smoother each time.

learn: Strong readers notice when they stop understanding. This is called monitoring.
When something is confusing, you can reread, read ahead, look at pictures, or use context clues.
Stopping to ask "What just happened?" every page or two keeps you on track.
check: What can you do when confused?
Which question keeps you on track?
lessons.try: While reading, stop after each page and retell what happened in one sentence.

learn: A reading log records the title, pages read and a short thought about each book.
Setting goals, like finishing one chapter book each week, builds reading habits.
Trying different genres, such as mystery, biography, fantasy and poetry, makes you a well-rounded reader.
check: What does a reading log record?
Title, pages and a short thought
lessons.try: Start a reading log and set a goal for this month.

learn: Strong readers read every day and choose books they enjoy.
They set a time and place for reading and protect it.
Reading twenty minutes a day adds up to over a million words a year.
check: Twenty minutes a day adds up to about a ___ words a year.
A good habit is to set a reading...
lessons.try: Make a reading-habit plan for this week.

learn: A genre is a kind of book: mystery, fantasy, biography, poetry, science.
Trying new genres stretches you as a reader.
Each genre has its own clues and features.
check: A genre is a ___ of book.
A true story of someone's life is a...
Trying new genres ___ you as a reader.
lessons.try: Read the first page of three books in different genres.

learn: Rate is how fast you read.
Read stories at a talking speed. Slow down for hard facts.
Too fast or too slow both make understanding harder.
lessons.try: Time yourself reading a page twice and compare.

learn: Phrasing means reading words in meaningful groups.
"The big dog / ran across / the yard" sounds better than word-by-word.
Punctuation tells you where to pause.
lessons.try: Mark phrases with slashes in a paragraph, then read it.

learn: Ask questions before, during and after reading.
"Why did she do that?" "What will happen?" "What does this word mean?"
Questions keep your brain active.
lessons.try: Write three questions on sticky notes while reading.

learn: Connect what you read to your life, other books and the world.
Text-to-self: "This reminds me of when I..."
Connections help you understand and remember.
check: "This reminds me of when I..." is a text-to-___ connection.
Linking two books is a text-to-___ connection.
lessons.try: Make one of each kind of connection for a story.

learn: An inference is using clues plus what you know to figure something out.
"She grabbed her umbrella" → it's probably raining.
Authors leave clues for you to find.
check: An inference uses clues plus what you...
"He yawned and rubbed his eyes" suggests he is...
lessons.try: Infer feelings from three picture clues.

learn: Use the author's words to build a picture in your mind.
Notice sense words: sights, sounds, smells, tastes, feelings.
Change the picture as you learn more.
check: Visualising means making a ___ in your mind.
Your mind picture should ___ as you learn more.
lessons.try: Sketch a scene from a chapter book.

learn: When something is confusing, reread it.
Read slower the second time.
Look for clues you missed.
lessons.try: Reread a tricky paragraph and explain it to a partner.

learn: Book talks help us understand more.
Share ideas, ask questions and listen to others.
Use evidence from the book: "On page 12 it says..."
check: In a book talk, you should ___ to others.
lessons.try: Hold a small book club talk.

learn: Stamina is reading for a long time without stopping.
Build it bit by bit: 15 minutes, then 20, then 30.
Remove distractions to focus.
check: Stamina means reading for a ___ time.
lessons.try: Track your reading stamina for a week.

learn: Look back at your reading log.
What did you read most? What did you enjoy?
Set a new goal for the next month.
check: A reading log helps you see your...
lessons.try: Write a reflection on your reading this unit.

learn: A prefix is a word part added to the beginning of a word that changes its meaning.
un- means not: unhappy. re- means again: reread. pre- means before: preview. dis- means opposite: disagree.
Knowing prefixes helps you figure out new words.
lessons.try: Add un-, re- or dis- to five words and write what each new word means.

learn: A suffix is added to the end of a word.
-ful means full of: hopeful. -less means without: fearless. -er can mean a person who: teacher. -ly often means in a way: slowly.
Sometimes spelling changes: happy becomes happily.
lessons.try: Find five words with suffixes in a book you're reading.

learn: Context clues are hints in the nearby words that help you understand a new word.
"The enormous elephant was so big it couldn't fit through the gate." The clue "so big" tells you enormous means very large.
A dictionary lists words in alphabetical order with their meanings and pronunciations.
lessons.try: Find a new word in a book, guess its meaning from context, then check a dictionary.

learn: A root word is the main part of a word.
In "unhappy" and "happiness," the root is happy.
Find the root to work out the meaning.
check: A root word is the ___ part of a word.
lessons.try: Circle the root in ten long words.

learn: un- means "not."
Unkind means not kind. Unlock means the opposite of lock.
Add un- to change a word's meaning.
lessons.try: Make five un- words.

learn: re- means "again."
Reread means read again. Rebuild means build again.
You use re- words every day.
lessons.try: Act out five re- words.

learn: pre- means "before": preview, preheat.
dis- means "not" or "opposite": dislike, disagree.
Prefixes change meaning at the start.
lessons.try: Sort words by prefix and meaning.

learn: mis- means "wrongly": misspell, misread.
non- means "not": nonstop, nonfiction.
Nonfiction is "not fiction" — true writing.
lessons.try: Fix sentences with mis- words.

learn: -ful means "full of": hopeful, careful.
-less means "without": hopeless, careless.
They are often opposites.
lessons.try: Make pairs: help, fear, use, care.

learn: -er, -or and -ist can mean "a person who."
Teacher, actor and artist.
These suffixes make job words.
check: A teacher is a person who...
lessons.try: Make job words from verbs.

learn: -ly makes adverbs: quick → quickly.
-ness makes nouns: kind → kindness.
Suffixes can change a word's job in a sentence.
lessons.try: Change five adjectives with -ly and -ness.

learn: Drop the final e before a vowel suffix: make → making.
Change y to i: happy → happiness.
Double the consonant in short words: run → running.
lessons.try: Add suffixes to ten words using the rules.

learn: Context clues are hints in nearby words.
"The arid desert had no water for months." Arid means dry.
Look for definitions, examples and opposites.
check: Context clues are hints in ___ words.
"The arid desert had no water" - arid means...
Context clues can be examples or...
lessons.try: Find meanings from context in five sentences.

learn: Dictionaries list words in ABC order with meanings and how to say them.
Words can have more than one meaning. Pick the one that fits.
Glossaries are found in nonfiction books.
check: If a word has many meanings, pick the one that...
lessons.try: Look up five multiple-meaning words.

learn: Roots carry meaning. Prefixes change the start. Suffixes change the end.
Context and dictionaries help with new words.
Breaking words apart is a reading superpower.
check: Unhelpful has a prefix, root and...
lessons.try: Build ten new words from roots, prefixes and suffixes.

learn: A character trait describes what a character is like inside: brave, honest, selfish, curious.
Traits are shown by actions and words. If a character returns a lost wallet, that shows honesty.
Always give evidence from the text for the traits you name.
check: What a character is like inside
What should you give for a trait?
lessons.try: Name two traits for a character in your book and give evidence for each.

learn: Motivation is why a character does something.
A character may act out of love, fear, jealousy or a wish to be accepted.
Understanding motivation helps you predict what the character will do next.
lessons.try: Explain why a character in your book made an important choice.

learn: A character's choices drive the plot forward.
In "The Boy Who Cried Wolf", the boy chooses to trick the villagers. When a real wolf comes, no one believes him.
Ask: what would have happened if the character chose differently?
check: Why didn't the villagers believe the boy?
Thinking about different choices helps you...
lessons.try: Rewrite the ending of a fable by changing one character's choice.

learn: Describe characters by how they look, act, speak and think.
Outside traits: tall, red-haired. Inside traits: brave, stubborn.
Inside traits matter most for understanding.
lessons.try: Make a character web for a main character.

learn: Back up a trait with evidence from the text.
"Max is generous because he gave his lunch away."
Find actions, words and thoughts as proof.
check: "He gave his lunch away" shows he is...
Proof can be actions, words or...
lessons.try: Write three traits with evidence for a character.

learn: Feelings change during a story.
A character might be nervous at first and proud at the end.
Track feelings on a chart.
check: Nervous at first and proud at the end shows...
You can track feelings on a...
lessons.try: Chart a character's feelings across a story.

learn: Motivation is why a character does something.
A character might want friendship, safety, revenge or a prize.
Motivation explains actions.
check: A character who is lonely might want...
lessons.try: Find what motivates three characters.

learn: Characters want something but face obstacles.
An obstacle is something in the way.
Stories get exciting when obstacles are big.
check: An obstacle is something in the...
lessons.try: List a character's want and three obstacles.

learn: Characters make choices that cause results.
A bad choice can cause trouble. A good choice can fix it.
Think: What would happen if the character chose differently?
check: Thinking about a different choice helps you...
lessons.try: Rewrite a scene with a different choice.

learn: A dynamic character changes. A static character stays the same.
Scrooge changes from greedy to generous.
Change usually comes from a lesson learned.
check: A character who stays the same is...
lessons.try: Compare a character at the beginning and the end.

learn: Characters are friends, rivals, family or strangers.
Relationships change during a story.
How characters treat each other shows who they are.
lessons.try: Draw a relationship map for a story.

learn: What characters say shows their personality.
A rude character speaks harshly. A shy one says little.
Read dialogue for clues.
lessons.try: Find a line of dialogue that shows a trait.

learn: Compare two characters with a Venn diagram.
How are they alike? How are they different?
Comparing deepens understanding.
check: Comparing shows how characters are alike and...
lessons.try: Compare two characters from different stories.

learn: First person uses "I". The narrator is a character.
Third person uses "he", "she", "they". The narrator is outside the story.
Your point of view may differ from the narrator's.
check: Your view may ___ from the narrator's.
lessons.try: Rewrite a paragraph from first to third person.

learn: Characters have traits, feelings and motivations.
Their choices drive the story and can change them.
Evidence from the text supports what you say.
check: Why a character acts is their...
lessons.try: Write a character analysis paragraph.

learn: A fable is a short tale, usually with animal characters, that teaches a moral.
Aesop was a storyteller in ancient Greece. His fables include "The Fox and the Grapes" and "The Lion and the Mouse".
In "The Lion and the Mouse", a tiny mouse frees a lion from a net. The moral: even small friends can be a big help.
lessons.try: Read "The Lion and the Mouse" and write its moral in your own words.

learn: Folktales are stories passed down by people telling them aloud for generations.
Many cultures have similar folktales. Cinderella stories exist in China (Yeh-Shen), Egypt (Rhodopis) and France.
Folktales often show a culture's values, like kindness or cleverness.
check: Yeh-Shen is a Cinderella story from...
lessons.try: Compare two Cinderella stories from different countries.

learn: A myth is a traditional story that explains something in nature or tells about gods and heroes.
The ancient Greeks told of Persephone, whose time below the earth each year explained winter.
Norse myths tell of Thor, whose hammer was said to make thunder.
check: What does a myth often explain?
In Norse myths, Thor's hammer made...
lessons.try: Write your own short myth explaining why the sky is blue.

learn: Traditional tales were passed down by telling.
Fables, folktales and myths are all traditional.
They teach lessons and explain the world.
check: Traditional tales were passed down by...
lessons.try: Ask an adult for a story they heard as a child.

learn: Aesop was a storyteller in ancient Greece.
His fables have animal characters and a moral.
"The Fox and the Grapes" teaches about pretending you don't want what you can't have.
check: In "The Fox and the Grapes," the fox pretends the grapes are...
lessons.try: Read two Aesop fables and state the morals.

learn: A thirsty crow can't reach water in a pitcher.
It drops pebbles in until the water rises.
Moral: little by little does the trick.
check: The crow drops ___ in the pitcher.
The water ___ as pebbles go in.
The moral is "little by little does the..."
lessons.try: Test the crow's idea with pebbles and a jar.

learn: Folktales show the beliefs of their culture.
Anansi stories come from West Africa. Momotaro comes from Japan.
Many share similar patterns.
check: Folktales show the beliefs of their...
lessons.try: Compare two folktales from different countries.

learn: Folktales often use the number three: three pigs, three wishes, three bears.
Good is rewarded and bad is punished.
They often begin "Once upon a time."
lessons.try: Find patterns in three folktales.

learn: Tall tales have heroes who are bigger than life.
Paul Bunyan was a giant lumberjack with a blue ox named Babe.
Tall tales use exaggeration for fun.
lessons.try: Write a tall-tale sentence about yourself.

learn: "Pourquoi" means "why" in French.
Pourquoi tales explain why things are: why the bear has a short tail.
They are made up, not science.
lessons.try: Write a pourquoi tale about an animal.

learn: Myths are ancient stories about gods and heroes.
They explain nature, like thunder or the seasons.
Greek, Norse and Egyptian myths are famous.
lessons.try: Read a myth that explains a season.

learn: Persephone was taken to the Underworld.
Her mother Demeter, goddess of harvest, grieved and plants died.
When Persephone returns, spring comes.
lessons.try: Draw the cycle of Persephone's story.

learn: Heroes go on quests and face monsters.
Hercules completed twelve labours.
Heroes show courage but also have flaws.
lessons.try: List a hero's strengths and flaws.

learn: Compare themes across fables, folktales and myths.
Many teach kindness, cleverness and courage.
The same message can appear in many cultures.
check: The same message can appear in many...
lessons.try: Make a chart comparing three tales' themes.

learn: Write your own fable, pourquoi tale or tall tale.
Use patterns: three tries, a lesson, a big hero.
Share it aloud like the old storytellers.
lessons.try: Write and tell your traditional tale.

learn: The main idea is the most important point the author wants you to understand.
Sometimes it's stated in a topic sentence. Sometimes you have to figure it out from the details.
Ask: what is this mostly about?
check: Where is the main idea sometimes stated?
lessons.try: Read a nonfiction article and write its main idea in one sentence.

learn: Key details are facts, examples or reasons that support the main idea.
If the main idea is "Bats are helpful animals", details might be "Bats eat insects" and "Bats pollinate plants".
Not every detail is key. Some are interesting but don't support the main idea.
lessons.try: List three key details that support your main idea.

learn: A summary is a short retelling of the main idea and key details in your own words.
Leave out small details and opinions.
A good summary is much shorter than the original.
check: A short retelling in your own words
A copy of the whole text
What should a summary leave out?
lessons.try: Write a three-sentence summary of a short article.

learn: The topic is what a text is about in a word or two: sharks.
The main idea is the most important point: Sharks are skilled hunters.
The main idea is a full sentence.
check: The main idea is a full...
lessons.try: Name the topic and main idea of three paragraphs.

learn: The main idea is often in the first sentence.
Sometimes it's at the end or not stated at all.
If not stated, you put it in your own words.
check: The main idea is often in the ___ sentence.
If not stated, put it in your...
lessons.try: Find the main idea sentence in five paragraphs.

learn: Details give facts, examples and reasons.
They tell more about the main idea.
Each detail should connect to the main idea.
check: Each detail should ___ to the main idea.
lessons.try: List three details for a main idea.

learn: Think of a table: the top is the main idea, the legs are details.
Without legs, the table falls.
Draw tables to organise ideas.
check: In the table model, the top is the...
lessons.try: Draw a main-idea table for a paragraph.

learn: Some sentences don't support the main idea.
In a paragraph about bees, "My aunt likes jam" doesn't belong.
Cross out sentences that don't fit.
check: In a paragraph about bees, which doesn't belong?
Sentences that don't fit should be...
lessons.try: Find the sentence that doesn't belong in five paragraphs.

learn: Each paragraph has a main idea.
Together they support the main idea of the whole text.
Headings give clues.
check: Paragraph main ideas support the ___ main idea.
lessons.try: Find each paragraph's main idea, then the whole text's.

lessons.t: Main Idea in Pictures and Charts
learn: Pictures and charts have main ideas too.
A chart of rainfall shows which month is wettest.
Ask: What is this picture mostly showing?
check: Ask what a picture is ___ showing.
A rainfall chart shows the ___ month.
lessons.try: State the main idea of three graphs.

learn: A summary retells the most important parts briefly.
It uses your own words.
It leaves out small details and opinions.
lessons.try: Read a summary and compare it to the full text.

learn: State the main idea, then two or three key details.
Keep it to a few sentences.
Don't copy whole sentences.
lessons.try: Write a three-sentence summary of an article.

learn: Use Somebody–Wanted–But–So–Then.
"Goldilocks wanted porridge, but it was too hot, so she tried others, then the bears came home."
It keeps summaries short.
lessons.try: Summarise a story with Somebody–Wanted–But–So–Then.

learn: Paraphrasing is saying one idea in your own words.
Read, cover the text, then write it your way.
Check you kept the meaning.
check: After writing, check you kept the...
lessons.try: Paraphrase five sentences.

learn: Topic, main idea, details and summaries work together.
Find the main idea, support it, then summarise.
These skills help in every subject.
check: The most important point is the...
lessons.try: Teach a younger student how to find the main idea.

learn: Text features help readers find and understand information.
Headings, subheadings, bold words, captions, maps, diagrams, timelines and sidebars are all text features.
A sidebar is a box with extra information next to the main text.
lessons.try: Find five different text features in a nonfiction book.

learn: Authors organise information in structures.
Sequence tells steps in order. Compare and contrast shows how things are alike and different. Cause and effect explains why something happens.
Problem and solution describes a problem and how it was solved.
check: Which structure tells steps in order?
Which structure shows how things are alike and different?
lessons.try: Read a short article and name its structure.

learn: Signal words help you spot the structure.
First, next, finally signal sequence. Because, so, as a result signal cause and effect.
Both, however, unlike signal compare and contrast.
lessons.try: Underline signal words in a paragraph.

learn: Titles name the whole text. Headings name sections. Subheadings split sections more.
Skim headings first to preview the text.
Headings help you find facts fast.
lessons.try: Preview an article by reading only its headings.

learn: A sidebar is a box with extra facts beside the main text.
Callouts point to parts of a picture.
Read them after the main text or when you need them.
check: Callouts point to parts of a...
lessons.try: Find sidebars in three nonfiction books.

learn: Maps show where. Timelines show when. Tables organise numbers.
Each feature adds facts.
Always read the title and labels.
lessons.try: Answer three questions using a timeline.

learn: Search tools help find information.
Keywords, the index and hyperlinks are search tools.
Choose keywords carefully.
lessons.try: Use an index and a keyword search to find the same fact.

learn: Text structure is how a writer organises information.
Five common structures: description, sequence, compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution.
Knowing structure helps you understand.
check: Text structure is how information is...
How many common structures are there?
lessons.try: Sort five short paragraphs by structure.

learn: Description tells what something is like.
Signal words: for example, such as, looks like.
Use a web to organise description.
lessons.try: Read a descriptive paragraph and make a web.

learn: Sequence tells events or steps in order.
Signal words: first, next, then, after, finally.
Use a numbered list or timeline.
lessons.try: Read a how-to text and number the steps.

learn: Compare shows how things are alike. Contrast shows how they differ.
Signal words: both, alike, however, but, unlike.
Use a Venn diagram.
check: Use a ___ for compare and contrast.
lessons.try: Read about frogs and toads and fill a Venn diagram.

learn: A cause is why something happens. The effect is what happens.
Signal words: because, so, as a result, since.
"Because it rained, the game was cancelled."
check: "Because it rained, the game was cancelled." The effect is...
lessons.try: Find three cause-effect pairs in an article.

learn: Problem/solution explains a problem and how it was fixed.
Signal words: problem, solution, solved, fixed.
Example: litter in parks → recycling bins added.
check: Recycling bins in parks could solve...
lessons.try: Read about a community problem and its solution.

learn: Signal words are clues to structure.
Highlight them as you read.
They make reading faster and clearer.
lessons.try: Highlight signal words in two articles.

learn: Text features help you find information.
Structures help you understand how it's organised.
Use both to read nonfiction like an expert.
check: A box with extra facts is a...
lessons.try: Make a reference card of features and structures.

learn: Pronouns replace nouns: he, she, it, they, we.
Subjects and verbs must agree: "The dog runs." "The dogs run."
Pronouns must match their nouns: "Maria lost her hat."
lessons.try: Rewrite a paragraph using pronouns to avoid repeating names.

learn: Comparatives compare two things: taller, faster, more careful.
Superlatives compare three or more: tallest, fastest, most careful.
Some are irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst.
check: The ___ of the three runners won.
lessons.try: Compare three animals using -er and -est words.

learn: Use commas in a list: "I packed socks, shoes, and a hat."
Use commas in addresses: Austin, Texas.
Quotation marks go around exact words someone says: "Let's go," said Ana.
check: Where do commas go in a list?
What goes around someone's exact words?
lessons.try: Write a short conversation between two characters with correct punctuation.

learn: Nouns name people, places, things and ideas.
Abstract nouns name ideas you can't touch: courage, love, freedom.
Concrete nouns name things you can touch.
lessons.try: Sort nouns into concrete and abstract.

learn: Add 's to a singular noun to show ownership: the dog's bone.
Add just ' to plural nouns ending in s: the dogs' bones.
Irregular plurals add 's: the children's toys.
lessons.try: Write five possessive phrases.

learn: Pronouns must match the noun they replace.
"The girls lost their hats," not "her hats."
Singular nouns take singular pronouns.
lessons.try: Fix five pronoun mistakes.

learn: Singular subjects take singular verbs: The dog runs.
Plural subjects take plural verbs: The dogs run.
Listen to see if it sounds right.
lessons.try: Choose the right verb in ten sentences.

learn: Past, present and future tenses show time.
I walked. I walk. I will walk.
Keep tense the same in a paragraph.
lessons.try: Rewrite a paragraph in the future tense.

learn: Some verbs change completely in the past: go/went, eat/ate, bring/brought.
Learn them by practice.
Wrong: "I goed." Right: "I went."
lessons.try: Play an irregular verb memory game.

learn: Adjectives describe nouns.
When using several, follow an order: number, opinion, size, colour.
"Two lovely big red apples."
lessons.try: Write five noun phrases with three adjectives.

learn: -er compares two: faster. -est compares three or more: fastest.
Long adjectives use more/most: more beautiful, most beautiful.
Some are irregular: good, better, best.
lessons.try: Compare three animals with -er, -est, more and most.

learn: Adverbs tell how, when, where or how often.
She sang beautifully. We left early. They play outside. He always smiles.
Many adverbs end in -ly, but not all.
lessons.try: Add an adverb to ten sentences.

learn: FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
They join two sentences with a comma before.
"I was tired, so I went to bed."
lessons.try: Join five pairs with FANBOYS.

learn: because, when, if, although, after, before join a main and a helper clause.
"When the bell rang, we lined up."
Put a comma after the helper clause when it comes first.
check: "When the bell rang, we lined up." The comma comes after...
lessons.try: Write five complex sentences.

learn: Put quotation marks around spoken words.
Commas and end marks go inside the quotes: "Let's go," said Ana.
New speaker, new paragraph.
lessons.try: Punctuate a short dialogue.

learn: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea.
The topic sentence tells the main idea of the paragraph, often at the start.
A strong topic sentence makes readers want to keep reading.
check: What does a topic sentence tell?
lessons.try: Write three different topic sentences about your favourite animal.

learn: Supporting sentences give facts, examples and details about the topic.
Most paragraphs have three to five supporting sentences.
Every sentence should connect to the topic.
check: Should every sentence connect to the topic?
Most paragraphs have about how many supporting sentences?
lessons.try: Write a paragraph with a topic sentence and three supporting sentences.

learn: Transitions connect ideas: also, for example, in addition, another reason.
A closing sentence wraps up the paragraph.
The closing often restates the main idea in new words.
check: What does a closing sentence do?
lessons.try: Add transitions and a closing sentence to your paragraph.

learn: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea.
It starts on a new line, often indented.
Paragraphs make writing easier to read.
lessons.try: Count the paragraphs in an article and name each idea.

learn: A topic sentence tells the main idea.
Make it interesting: "Penguins are birds that can't fly but swim like rockets."
Avoid "This paragraph is about..."
lessons.try: Rewrite three boring topic sentences.

learn: Facts can be proved: "Penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere."
Use facts from reliable sources.
Two to four facts make a strong paragraph.
lessons.try: Add three facts to a topic sentence.

learn: Examples show what you mean.
"Many birds can't fly, for example penguins, ostriches and emus."
Examples make ideas clear.
lessons.try: Write a paragraph with two examples.

learn: After a detail, explain why it matters.
"Penguins have thick feathers. This keeps them warm in icy water."
Explanations add depth.
check: After a detail, explain why it...
lessons.try: Add an explanation sentence to three details.

learn: Transitions link sentences: also, in addition, for example, however, finally.
They help ideas flow.
Don't use the same one every time.
lessons.try: Add transitions to a choppy paragraph.

learn: A closing sentence wraps up the paragraph.
Restate the main idea in new words.
"Penguins truly are amazing swimmers."
lessons.try: Write closing sentences for three paragraphs.

learn: Top bun: topic sentence. Fillings: details. Bottom bun: closing.
Each part has a job.
The model helps plan writing.
lessons.try: Plan a paragraph on a hamburger organiser.

learn: How-to paragraphs give steps in order.
Use sequence transitions: first, next, then, finally.
Include all steps clearly.
lessons.try: Write a how-to paragraph for making a sandwich.

learn: Compare paragraphs show likenesses and differences.
Use both, also, but, unlike.
Keep comparisons balanced.
lessons.try: Write a paragraph comparing two pets.

learn: Indent the first line of each paragraph.
Start a new paragraph for a new idea.
Organised writing is easier to follow.
check: Start a new paragraph for a new...
lessons.try: Split a long block of text into paragraphs.

learn: Topic sentence, supporting details, explanations, transitions and a closing.
One idea per paragraph.
Revise to make it clear and lively.
lessons.try: Write and revise a paragraph on any topic.

learn: A good narrative has characters, a setting, a problem, events and a resolution.
Plan with a story mountain: beginning, rising action, climax, falling action, ending.
The climax is the most exciting point, where the problem is faced.
lessons.try: Draw a story mountain for a story you want to write.

learn: Instead of telling "Sam was scared," show it: "Sam's knees shook and his voice came out as a whisper."
Use the senses: what do characters see, hear, smell, taste and feel?
Dialogue and action bring characters to life.
check: Which shows that Sam was scared?
lessons.try: Rewrite "It was a hot day" by showing, not telling.

learn: A strong ending solves the problem and shows how the character feels or changed.
Revise by reading aloud and asking: Is it clear? Is it exciting? Does it make sense?
Edit for spelling, capitals and punctuation last.
lessons.try: Revise your story, then ask someone to read it and give one suggestion.

learn: Great stories often begin with real moments.
A lost tooth, a big storm, a new pet.
Add "What if?" to make it more exciting.
check: A lost tooth could be a...
lessons.try: List five small moments and pick one to grow.

learn: Give your character a want, a fear and a flaw.
A flaw makes them real and interesting.
Readers care about characters with feelings.
check: Give your character a want, fear and...
lessons.try: Make a character card with want, fear and flaw.

learn: Use five senses to describe the setting.
Weather and time of day add mood.
Setting can create problems.
check: Use your five ___ to describe setting.
lessons.try: Write a setting paragraph using all five senses.

learn: A plot climbs like a mountain.
Beginning, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
The climax is the most exciting point.
check: The most exciting point is the...
Events that build tension are the...
lessons.try: Plan your story on a plot mountain.

learn: Hook readers with action, dialogue, a question or a surprising fact.
Start in the middle of something happening.
Skip long introductions.
check: Start in the ___ of the action.
lessons.try: Write three hooks and pick the best.

learn: Show feelings through body language: clenched fists, a trembling voice.
Let readers infer.
Showing makes stories vivid.
lessons.try: Turn five "telling" lines into "showing" lines.

learn: Dialogue should reveal character or move the plot.
Use said, asked, whispered, shouted.
Don't let characters talk about nothing.
lessons.try: Write a dialogue that reveals a secret.

learn: Pacing is how fast a story moves.
Slow down for important moments with details.
Speed up boring parts with a sentence: "Three days later..."
check: Pacing is how fast a story...
lessons.try: Slow down the climax of your story.

learn: Strong verbs show action clearly: sprinted instead of ran fast.
Precise nouns name exactly: poodle instead of dog.
Both make writing vivid.
check: A stronger verb than "ran fast" is...
lessons.try: Replace ten weak words in your draft.

learn: A good ending solves the problem.
Show how the character changed.
Leave the reader with a feeling.
check: Endings can show how the character...
lessons.try: Write two endings and choose the best.

learn: Partners give stars (what works) and wishes (what to improve).
Listen without arguing.
Choose changes that make the story better.
lessons.try: Give and get two stars and a wish.

learn: Edit for spelling, capitals and punctuation.
Make a neat final copy with a title and illustrations.
Share it with an audience.
lessons.try: Publish your story in a class anthology.

learn: An opinion essay states a clear opinion, gives reasons with examples, and ends with a conclusion.
Linking words like because, therefore, since and for example connect opinions and reasons.
Strong reasons are supported by facts, not just feelings.
lessons.try: Write an opinion essay: Should students have homework?

learn: Research starts with a question: How do bees make honey?
Use several sources: books, encyclopaedias and trusted websites ending in .gov or .edu.
Take notes in your own words and record the source.
check: Which is often a trusted website ending?
lessons.try: Research a question and take notes from two sources.

learn: A report has an introduction, body paragraphs on subtopics, and a conclusion.
Each body paragraph covers one subtopic, like what bees eat or how they make hives.
List your sources at the end.
check: A report has an introduction, body and...
lessons.try: Turn your research notes into a three-paragraph report.

learn: An opinion statement takes a clear side.
"Schools should have longer recess."
Avoid "maybe" or "kind of."
check: A strong opinion takes a clear...
lessons.try: Write strong opinions on three topics.

learn: Give reasons and support them with facts or examples.
"Longer recess helps kids focus. Studies show exercise improves attention."
More evidence makes a stronger case.
lessons.try: Find evidence for each reason.

learn: Linking words connect opinions and reasons.
Because, therefore, since, for example, in addition.
They make writing flow and convince.
lessons.try: Add linking words to an opinion paragraph.

learn: The introduction hooks and states your opinion.
The conclusion restates it and leaves a final thought.
Both frame your writing.
lessons.try: Write an introduction and conclusion for an opinion essay.

learn: A persuasive letter asks someone to do something.
Be polite and give strong reasons.
Write to the principal, mayor or a company.
check: A persuasive letter asks someone to...
lessons.try: Write a persuasive letter to the principal.

learn: Pick a topic you're curious about.
Make it not too big: "Animals" is too big; "How bats find food" is better.
Write questions you want answered.
lessons.try: Narrow a big topic to a good research question.

learn: Use books, encyclopedias and trusted websites.
Check who wrote it and when.
Use at least two sources.
lessons.try: Find two sources for your research question.

lessons.t: Taking Notes in Your Own Words
learn: Write key words, not whole sentences.
Sort notes by question or subtopic.
Write where each note came from.
lessons.try: Take notes on index cards sorted by subtopic.

learn: Introduction, body paragraphs (one per subtopic) and conclusion.
Use headings for each section.
Add a picture or diagram.
lessons.try: Outline your report.

learn: Turn your notes into sentences and paragraphs.
Explain facts so readers understand.
Use your own words throughout.
lessons.try: Draft your report from your outline.

learn: List the sources you used at the end.
Write the title and author of each.
This gives credit and lets readers check.
check: Write the title and ___ of each source.
lessons.try: Write a sources list for your report.

learn: Practise reading your report aloud.
Speak clearly, look at your audience and show visuals.
Answer questions politely.
lessons.try: Present your report to the class.
